title: The zoom lever, and the ingredient that runs out first
summary: Slide powers of ten up to the nearest star and down to a grain of dust, cash in the negative exponents, then take the month's monster at walking pace and find where the zeros on the end of a huge product actually come from. The week ends outside with the star wheel.
materials: planisphere or star wheel, the one made for your latitude
field journal, pencil and a ruler
a clear night, the porch light off, and something warm to sit on

problems.prompt: A thousand thousands is a million. Written out in full, how many zeros does a million have?
explanation: A thousand is a 1 with three zeros behind it.
A thousand of those is those three zeros joined by three more.
So a million is a 1 with six zeros behind it.
problems.useAgain: when a big round number needs sizing and counting its zeros is faster than reading it out.
hints: Write a thousand out in full first and count what is behind the 1.
Multiplying by a thousand puts three more zeros on the end.
problems.socraticHint: When two round numbers are multiplied, do their zeros join up, or is that just a coincidence here?

variant.prompt: A thousand millions is a billion. Written out in full, how many zeros does a billion have?

problems.prompt: Which is bigger: 2 to the power 10, which is ten 2s multiplied together, or 10 to the power 3, which is three 10s multiplied together?
explanation: Ten 2s multiplied together come to 1024.
Three 10s multiplied together come to 1000.
The small base with the big exponent wins, by 24, which is why you work both out instead of trusting the bigger looking number.
problems.useAgain: when two powers have different bases and different exponents, so neither can be read off at a glance.
hints: Neither one is obvious from looking, so both of them have to be worked out.
Double 2 ten times, writing down where you get to each time.
problems.socraticHint: If you added 1 to each exponent, which of the two would grow by more?

variant.prompt: Which is bigger: 5 to the power 3, which is three 5s multiplied together, or 3 to the power 5, which is five 3s multiplied together?

explanation: Multiplying by 10,000 slides every digit four places to the left.
The 1 in 0.001 sits three places behind the point, so four places to the left puts it one place in front of it.
One place in front of the point is 10.
problems.useAgain: when a small decimal meets a big round number and the digits only need moving, not multiplying.
hints: Count how many places the point has to travel, and which way.
Multiplying by ten once moves everything one place to the left. Do that four times.
problems.socraticHint: Before working it out, is the answer going to be bigger or smaller than 1, and what tells you?

problem.prompt: A sugar cube is 1 centimetre on every side. You stack sugar cubes into one big solid cube that is 10 centimetres on every side. How many sugar cubes does it take?
explanation: One flat layer of the big cube is 10 cubes along and 10 cubes across, which is 100 sugar cubes.
The big cube is 10 layers tall, so it holds 10 lots of 100.
That is 1000, and it is the zoom lever at work. One notch of ten in each of three directions is three notches, and three notches of ten is a thousand.
The trap is answering 10, or 100. Ten times bigger in every direction is nothing like ten times more stuff.
problem.useAgain: when something grows by the same factor in more than one direction at once and you need what happened to the whole of it.
hints: Build one flat layer in your head before you try to see the whole block.
Count the cubes in one layer, then count how many of those layers stand on top of each other.
problem.socraticHint: If the big cube were only twice as wide, twice as deep and twice as tall, would it hold twice as much?

variant.prompt: A sugar cube is 1 centimetre on every side. You stack them into a solid cube 100 centimetres on every side, which is a metre in each direction. How many sugar cubes does it take?

steps.title: The zoom lever: powers of ten, up to the stars and down to the dust

problems.prompt: The Sun is about 93,000,000 miles away. Which of these is that distance written in scientific notation?
explanation: Scientific notation allows one non-zero digit in front of the point, so the front number sits between 1 and 10.
Slide the point from the end of 93,000,000 until it lands between the 9 and the 3, which takes seven places. The distance is therefore 9.3 times 10 to the 7.
The last two options are the right distance and still wrong: 93 is too big for the front, 0.93 too small.
problems.useAgain: when a number is too long to read at a glance and only its size and its first digits matter.
hints: Two of these options are the right distance. Ask what the rule says about the front number.
Count the places the point has to move, one at a time, and keep the count.
problems.socraticHint: What is the rule doing for you by insisting the front number sits between 1 and 10?

variant.prompt: Light travels about 300,000,000 metres every second. Which of these is that speed written in scientific notation?

problems.prompt:
Chen wrote 0.000047 in scientific notation like this:
Line 1: Move the decimal point until exactly one non-zero digit sits in front of it: 4.7.
Line 2: Count the places the point moved: 1, 2, 3, 4. Four places.
Line 3: Since the original number is smaller than 1, the exponent is negative: 4.7 times 10 to the negative 4.
Line 4: Check: 4.7 times 10 to the negative 4 is 0.00047.
Which line is wrong?
explanation: Line 2 is wrong: the point actually moves five places to land between the 4 and the 7, not four.
Line 1 is correct: 4.7 is the right front number, with exactly one non-zero digit before the point.
Lines 3 and 4 are done correctly for the count they were given. They just inherited Line 2's short count.
The true answer is 4.7 times 10 to the negative 5, since 0.000047 has five places between its decimal point and the 4.
problems.useAgain: when you write a small decimal in scientific notation and need to count exactly how many places the point moved.
hints: Count the places one at a time, out loud, rather than guessing the count by eye.
Every zero between the decimal point and the first non-zero digit counts as one place moved.
problems.socraticHint: If you moved the point back the number of places you counted, would you land exactly on the original number?

variant.prompt:
Yara converted 6.2 times 10 to the 4th into an ordinary number like this:
Line 1: A positive exponent of 4 means the point moves 4 places to the left.
Line 2: Move the point 4 places to the left: 0.00062.
Line 3: Check by counting zeros: 0.00062 has the point sitting four places from the 6.
Line 4: So 6.2 times 10 to the 4th equals 0.00062.
Which line is wrong?

problems.prompt: Multiply 4 times 10 to the 3 by 2 times 10 to the 5. The answer comes out as 8 times 10 to the power of something. What is that power?
explanation: Deal with the front numbers on their own: 4 times 2 is 8.
Now the tens. Three tens in a row times five tens in a row is eight tens in a row.
So the answer is 8 times 10 to the 8. Check: 4000 times 200,000 is 800,000,000.
The trap is multiplying the exponents instead of adding them.
problems.useAgain: when two numbers in scientific notation are multiplied and the tens can be handled apart from the digits.
hints: Split the job in two: the front numbers, then the tens.
Write out what 10 to the 3 and 10 to the 5 actually are, side by side, and count the tens you are holding.
problems.socraticHint: If exponents were multiplied here, what would 10 to the 1 times 10 to the 1 have to come to?

variant.prompt: Multiply 3 times 10 to the 4 by 3 times 10 to the 6. The answer comes out as 9 times 10 to the power of something. What is that power?

problems.prompt: A grain of fine dust is about 2 times 10 to the negative 5 metres across. Laid in a line, touching, how many grains would it take to stretch one metre?
explanation: First cash in the exponent: 2 times 10 to the negative 5 is 0.00002 metres.
The question is how many 0.00002s fit inside 1, so share 1 by 0.00002.
Fifty thousand of them, and the check is quick: 50,000 times 0.00002 is 1.
problems.useAgain: when a tiny measurement is written with a negative power and you need how many of them make one whole unit.
hints: Write the grain's size out as an ordinary decimal before you do anything else with it.
This is a sharing question: one metre shared into pieces that size.
problems.socraticHint: Is the answer going to be bigger or smaller than a thousand, and what tells you that before you divide?

variant.prompt: A grain is about 5 times 10 to the negative 5 metres across. Laid in a line, touching, how many grains would it take to stretch one metre?

problems.prompt: The Sun is about 1.5 times 10 to the 11 metres away. A person is about 1.5 metres tall. Lying head to toe, about how many people would reach the Sun? The answer is 10 to the power of something. What is that power?
explanation: Share the distance by one person's height: 1.5 times 10 to the 11, shared by 1.5.
The two front numbers are identical, so they cancel and leave nothing but the tens.
What is left is 10 to the 11, a hundred thousand million people.
Numbers chosen so they cancel are a gift. Look for them before reaching for a calculator.
problems.useAgain: when a huge measurement is compared with an everyday one and only the number of tens between them matters.
hints: Write the division down before you calculate anything, and look hard at the two front numbers.
Handle the front numbers first and see what is left over.
problems.socraticHint: What would change about the answer if the person were 3 metres tall instead?

variant.prompt: A city block is about 1.5 times 10 to the 2 metres long. A person is about 1.5 metres tall. Lying head to toe, about how many people would reach along one block? The answer is 10 to the power of something. What is that power?

problems.prompt: A light year is about 9.5 times 10 to the 12 kilometres. The nearest star after the Sun is about 4.2 light years away. Roughly how far is that in kilometres?
explanation: The question says roughly, so round the front numbers hard: about 4 lots of about 9.5 is about 40.
That gives 40 times 10 to the 12, which is not scientific notation.
Slide one more place: that is 4 times 10 to the 13.

Two of the wrong options are a whole notch of ten out, one too close and one too far. A notch of ten is never a small mistake here, and the last option keeps the right notch but spoils the front number.
problems.useAgain: when a question says roughly, so the digits can be rounded hard as long as the tens are counted exactly.
hints: Round 9.5 and 4.2 to something you can multiply in your head before you touch the tens.
Your first answer will probably have a front number bigger than 10. That is fine, it just needs tidying.
problems.socraticHint: If your rounding was out by a tenth of the number, could that ever move the answer to a different power of ten?

variant.prompt: A light year is about 9.5 times 10 to the 12 kilometres. The brightest star in the night sky is about 8.6 light years away. Roughly how far is that in kilometres?

steps.title: Co-interior and the parallelogram's neighbor, and winning with or without the condition

problems.prompt: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, making a 48 degree angle on one line. What is the co-interior (same-side interior) angle on the other line, in degrees?
explanation: Co-interior angles sit on the same side of the transversal, between the two parallel lines.
Unlike corresponding or alternate angles, co-interior angles add up to 180 degrees, not match each other.
180 minus 48 is 132 degrees.
problems.useAgain: when two angles sit on the same side between parallel lines, since co-interior angles are supplementary, not equal.
hints: Do co-interior angles match each other, or add up to something?
Subtract the given angle from 180.
problems.socraticHint: Is every pair of angles made by a transversal on parallel lines equal, or do some pairs add to 180 instead?

variant.prompt: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, making a 112 degree angle on one line. What is the co-interior angle on the other line, in degrees?

problems.prompt: A parallelogram has one angle measuring 65 degrees. Its opposite sides are parallel. What is the angle adjacent to it, sharing a side, in degrees?
explanation: Two adjacent angles in a parallelogram sit like co-interior angles between its parallel sides.
That means they always add up to 180 degrees.
180 minus 65 is 115 degrees.
problems.useAgain: when a parallelogram's neighboring angles are treated as co-interior angles between its own parallel sides.
hints: Adjacent angles in a parallelogram behave like which kind of parallel-line angle pair?
Subtract the known angle from 180.
problems.socraticHint: Since a parallelogram's opposite sides are two parallel lines, what relationship do its two neighboring angles share?

variant.prompt: A parallelogram has one angle measuring 100 degrees. What is the angle adjacent to it, sharing a side, in degrees?

problems.prompt: A team's records: of 25 players who practiced extra, 18 won their game. Of 25 who did not, 10 won. Of players who practiced extra, what fraction won?
explanation: The condition here is having practiced extra, so only that group of 25 forms the whole.
18 out of those 25 won, giving the fraction 18/25.
The players who did not practice extra do not enter this particular fraction at all.
problems.useAgain: when a condition names one specific group, and only that group's own total is used in the fraction.
hints: Which group of 25 does the condition point you to?
Put the number of wins from that exact group over its own total.
problems.socraticHint: Does the number of wins from the non-practicing group belong anywhere in this fraction?

variant.prompt: A team's records: of 25 players who practiced extra, 20 won their game. Of 25 who did not, 5 won. Of players who practiced extra, what fraction won?

problems.prompt: Using the same records (18 of 25 practiced-players won, 10 of 25 non-practiced players won), what fraction of all 50 players won, regardless of practice?
explanation: This time there is no condition, so all 50 players form the whole.
Total wins across both groups is 18 plus 10, which is 28.
28 out of 50 simplifies to 14/25, a different, smaller-looking fraction than either group's own rate.
problems.useAgain: when comparing a plain, unconditional rate to a conditional one drawn from the exact same records.
hints: This question drops the practice condition entirely; whose wins and whose total belong in it now?
Add both groups' wins and both groups' totals before dividing.
problems.socraticHint: Does removing the practice condition change which players' records belong in the count?

variant.prompt: Using records where 20 of 25 practiced-players won and 10 of 25 non-practiced players won, what fraction of all 50 players won, regardless of practice?

steps.title: The monster at walking pace: where the zeros on the end come from

problems.prompt: Invent your own trailing-zeros puzzle: pick a range of consecutive whole numbers to multiply together, different from 1 through 10, 20 or 25, which are already used this week. Work out yourself how many zeros the product ends in, then write the puzzle down with your one correct answer. Prove your total by listing every multiple of five in your range, checking each one for a hidden second five the way 25 hid one, and confirming there are enough twos left over to pair with every five you found.

mustMention: the range of numbers I chose
the number of zeros I found
every multiple of five in my range, including any hiding a second five
enough twos to pair with every five

explanation: A trailing-zeros puzzle only works if you already know the true answer before anyone else tries it.
List every multiple of five in your chosen range first, since fives are the scarce ingredient that decides the count.
Check each one honestly: a number like 25 or 50 hides more than one five inside it, and missing that gives a wrong total.
Twos are always plentiful enough to pair with every five you found, so the fives alone set your final answer.
problems.useAgain: when you want to set your own version of a puzzle and have to prove your own answer is the only right one.
hints: Pick a range nobody has used this week yet, and work out your own answer before you write the puzzle down.
List the multiples of five in your range one at a time, and check each one for a hidden extra five.
problems.socraticHint: If a friend picked a totally different range, would the same method still tell them their answer for sure?

problems.prompt: Multiply the whole numbers 1 through 20 together. How many zeros does the answer end in? You are not expected to work out the product itself.
explanation: Same hunt as before, and this time the point is that you never touch the actual product.
The fives in 1 through 20 are 5, 10, 15 and 20. Four of them.
Even numbers are far more common, so there is a two waiting for every one of those fives.
Four pairs, so four zeros, and the answer has nineteen digits that nobody had to work out.
problems.useAgain: when the product is far too big to compute and only one feature of it is being asked for.
hints: Do not multiply anything. List instead.
Write down every number in the list that carries a five inside it.
problems.socraticHint: Does the size of that product make this harder, or does it only make it look harder?

variant.prompt: Multiply the whole numbers 1 through 19 together. How many zeros does the answer end in?

problems.prompt: Inside the product of 1 through 20 there are eighteen twos but only four fives. So it is the fives, not the twos, that decide how many zeros the answer ends in. True or false?
explanation: Count the twos honestly and the eighteen holds up. Ten even numbers give ten twos, then 4, 12 and 20 each hide a second one, 8 hides two more, and 16 hides three more.
Every zero on the end costs one two and one five, paired up.
Eighteen twos can only pair with as many fives as exist, and four exist.
So fourteen twos have nobody to pair with. The scarce ingredient sets the answer and the plentiful one never gets a vote.
problems.useAgain: when two things have to meet in pairs and you want to know which of them is the limit.
hints: Check the eighteen for yourself before deciding about the claim built on top of it.
Ask what one zero costs, in twos and in fives, then ask which one you run out of.
problems.socraticHint: If somebody handed you fourteen more twos, would a single extra zero appear?

variant.prompt: Inside the product of 1 through 30 there are more fives than twos, so it is the twos that decide how many zeros the answer ends in. True or false?

problems.prompt: Multiply the whole numbers 1 through 25 together. How many zeros does the answer end in? Count carefully, because this list has a surprise in it.
explanation: The multiples of five in the list are 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25, which is five of them.
But 25 is not carrying one five. It is 5 times 5, so it hands over two.
That makes six fives altogether, and there are twos to spare for all of them.
Six zeros. Counting the multiples of five is only the first pass. The second asks each one how many fives it holds.
problems.useAgain: when you are counting a factor and some numbers on your list quietly carry more than one of it.
hints: Count the multiples of five first, then go back and interrogate each one on its own.
Break every multiple of five into its prime factors and count the fives you can actually see.
problems.socraticHint: Is there a number on this list that is a five more than once over?

variant.prompt: Multiply the whole numbers 1 through 30 together. How many zeros does the answer end in?

problems.prompt: What is the smallest whole number n for which the product of 1 through n ends in exactly three zeros?
explanation: Zeros only arrive when a new five joins the list, so the count jumps at multiples of five and sits still in between.
1 through 14 holds the fives from 5 and 10, so two zeros. Bringing in 15 brings a third five.
So 15 is the first to reach three, and 16 through 19 all stay there.
Worth chasing on your own: no product of 1 through n ever ends in exactly five zeros. The reason is 25, the same surprise the 1 through 25 question had in it.
problems.useAgain: when you are hunting the first place a count reaches some value rather than the count itself.
hints: The zero count does not creep up one at a time. Find the places where it moves at all.
Work out the zeros for a few values of n in order and watch what your list of answers does.
problems.socraticHint: Between one multiple of five and the next, what happens to the number of zeros?

variant.prompt: What is the smallest whole number n for which the product of 1 through n ends in exactly four zeros?

problems.prompt: A peak, untimed. How many whole numbers between 99 and 999 have exactly one digit that is a zero?
explanation: Every number in the range has three digits, and the hundreds digit is never zero.
So the single zero is either in the tens place or in the units place, and it cannot be in both.
Zero in the tens place: 9 choices for the hundreds digit and 9 for the units, which must not be zero too. That is 81.
Zero in the units place: the same count the other way round, another 81.
81 and 81 is 162. The trap is letting numbers like 100 in, which have two zeros and not one.
problems.useAgain: when a condition can be met in a few separate ways and each way can be counted cleanly on its own.
hints: Which of the three digit places can never be the zero?
Split into cases by where the zero sits, count each case, then check that the cases cannot overlap.
problems.socraticHint: Does 100 belong in your count, and what exactly is the word exactly ruling out?

variant.prompt: A peak, untimed. How many whole numbers between 999 and 10000 have exactly one digit that is a zero?

steps.title: The star night, and the monster left on the shelf
steps.body:
Two short things, and both of them are meant to be light. This is the lightest week of the season in all three tracks, on purpose, because the weekend is the heavy thing.

The monster first. Factorial zeros has been on the Think home card since last week and it stays there. Nothing in today's lane finished it. The lane worked lists of ten, twenty, twenty-five and thirty, and the monster asks about one hundred. You now own every tool that question needs, and putting them together is yours to do, at the kitchen table, whenever you feel like it. Do not let anybody hand you the number. The oasis is where it gets settled, either resolved or retired with honours, and both of those are real endings.

Then the star night, which is where this week ends. Pick the clearest night, go out after dark, turn the porch light off and give your eyes a full twenty minutes to adjust before you judge the sky. That wait is not wasted time. Eyes genuinely keep getting better at the dark for half an hour or more, and almost everybody goes back inside before the good part.

Hold the planisphere up over your head rather than reading it like a book, and turn the wheel until tonight's date lines up with the time on the clock. What shows through the window is the sky above you. That is why the whole thing has to be turned: the sky turns too, about fifteen degrees an hour, because you are standing on something that is spinning.

Take the zoom lever outside with you. Before you go out, pick three stars and look up how far away each one is, then say the three distances out loud underneath them in powers of ten. Some are close, a few tens of light years. Some are thousands. And here is the honest part, worth saying under a real sky: for some bright stars the distance is genuinely argued about, and published estimates for the same star can differ by something close to a factor of two. Nobody has been there with a tape measure. A number with a real argument behind it is a better thing to know than a number that was only ever printed.

steps.title: Explain it in writing: the ladder from a dust grain to a star
steps.prompt: Build a size ladder in the field journal. Start at 10 to the negative 5 metres, about a grain of fine dust, and climb one rung at a time to 10 to the 17 metres, which is past the nearest star and past the brightest star in the night sky. Every rung is ten times the rung below it. Write the power of ten on every rung, and beside as many rungs as you can, name one real thing that is about that size. Some rungs will be easy and some will defeat you, and an empty rung with a question mark beside it is an honest rung. Then write two short paragraphs underneath. First: what a negative exponent is actually doing, in your own words, without using the word negative more than once. Second: pick any two rungs and say how many times bigger one is than the other, and show how you got that from the two powers alone, without writing either number out in full.

steps.title: Explain it out loud, under the sky
steps.prompt: Record this outside on the star night, with the planisphere in your hand. Explain to whoever is out there with you why the product of 1 through 25 ends in six zeros and not five. Take them through all of it: what makes a zero appear on the end at all, why you go hunting for fives rather than twos, and what 25 does that 5, 10, 15 and 20 do not. Then hand them the star wheel, get them to find one thing in the sky with it, and say out loud how far away it is in powers of ten.
